passage: A talus slope is a heap of broken rock at the foot of a cliff, and to a geologist its chief frustration is that it keeps no order: the boulder lying on top may have fallen last winter or a thousand years ago. Lichens can date an exposed rock face, but the summers on the Vetter Slope of the eastern Cascades are too dry for lichen, and the crews working there in the 1990s had no way to tell a young boulder from an old one. Dana Whitlock's crew looked instead at the side no one had examined, the underside, where the rock meets soil and a thin crust of mineral grains binds to it. That crust is tunneled by oribatid mites, which burrow into it at a rate that, unlike almost everything else on the slope, does not depend on the amount of rain the slope receives. Burrows accumulate and are not erased, so a boulder that has lain fast for a long time carries more of them per square centimeter than a recent arrival. To turn that into a clock, the crew needed rock of known age. An earthquake in 1924 had brought down a documented sheet of stone at the slope's northern end, and a logging road cut in 1961 had dumped a second, younger pile beside it. Counting burrows on eleven boulders from each gave a rate of about eleven burrows per square centimeter per century, and predicted the two known ages to within 4.2 percent. Whitlock is careful about the ceiling. Past about nine hundred years the crust itself begins to spall away, taking its burrows with it, so every older boulder returns the same saturated count. She calls the method good for a window rather than a chronology, and has refused to apply it to slopes whose soil chemistry differs from Vetter's until someone repeats the calibration there.

passage: Sleep is easy to recognize in a dog and hard to define in anything else, which is why researchers rely less on the word than on a checklist. Four conditions are usually required: the animal becomes less responsive to the world; the state reverses quickly when something important happens; it recurs on a daily rhythm; and, if the animal is kept from it, it takes more of it afterward. The fourth condition, called rebound, does the real work, because it separates sleep from stillness, and a stone is unresponsive but a stone does not catch up. Beroe pallens, a comb jelly of the cold water off southern Chile, has no brain at all; its nerve cells are spread through its body in a diffuse net. Ivar Lindqvist's laboratory kept forty under constant dim light and filmed the cilia along their combs, which normally beat without pause. Every animal slowed its beating for about ninety minutes, at the same point in each twenty-four-hour cycle, and returned to full speed within seconds when dye was released in the water near it. Three of the four conditions were met cleanly. The crew then kept the animals from slowing, using a gentle current timed to the onset of each quiet period, for three cycles. The rebound they recorded was four minutes, a quiet period ninety-four minutes long instead of ninety, a difference so small that Lindqvist reports the figure without building anything on it. The checklist as written admits no exception, and by it B. pallens does not sleep. Lindqvist's response was not to argue for the animal but to question the fourth condition. Rebound, he points out, is a way of detecting a cost: an animal that must make up lost sleep has paid for going without. In a creature with no brain to restore, the cost may be smaller, and a condition built around mammals would then be measuring the size of that debt rather than its existence. He has proposed replacing rebound with any demonstrated cost of staying awake, such as slower healing or poorer capture of prey, and the committee that maintains the checklist has taken the question up.

Halloway, a milling city on the Kesset, created the Office of the Ice Inspector in 1868, after two cutters and a team of horses went through thin ice at the lake's southern end. The figures were posted outside the market, so that cutters knew where to work and buyers knew what the season would cost. He measured in hands, a unit of four inches borrowed from the horse trade, and recorded the dates the ice first held a man and broke up. The office was abolished in 1911, three years after the Halloway Cold Storage Company opened a plant on the river and the lake harvest collapsed; the last inspector, Oyelaran, was moved to the weights and measures desk. passage: Arlen and Wyke sit nine miles apart on the same estuary, and for three centuries the difference between them was too small to interest anyone. Both had a tidal harbor, both sent out wool and barley and took in coal, and in 1850 they handled tonnages within a tenth of each other. In 1854 a branch line reached the estuary and, because the ground north of the river was firmer, ran to both towns. A railway at a port does not by itself move goods; it changes the place where goods are handed from one carrier to another, and the handing over is done by carts. Here the two towns differed, and the difference was old enough that nobody had thought of it as an economic policy. Arlen's carters had been a chartered company since 1611, and the charter reserved carriage within the town to men who had served a seven-year apprenticeship under a freeman of the company. Wyke had no such body; its carting had always been done by farmers in the slack season, and anyone with a horse could take a load. When the railway opened, a merchant in Wyke who wanted forty tons moved from a siding to a quay hired whoever was standing there. The same merchant in Arlen could hire only from a company of thirty-one men, whose number the charter fixed and whose rates it set. Within four years the estuary's transshipment trade had gathered at Wyke; by 1861 Wyke was handling three and a half times Arlen's tonnage, and the warehouses rising along the new sidings were rising there. Arlen's company saw the problem and petitioned to open its rolls in 1866, and the charter was amended in 1869. It made no difference. The warehouses, the bonded stores and the agents' offices were in Wyke by then, and they were not going to be moved nine miles because carting in Arlen had become cheaper. The comparison is useful precisely because the two towns are otherwise so alike; it is hard to find another case in which the want of a single rule is so nearly the only variable.
